performers: Sergei Rachmaninoff, piano; Philadelphia Orchestra; Leopold Stokowski, conductor
intro: Rachmaninoff accompanies the flute and clarinet in the opening song of his Adagio, with Leopold Stokowski conducting the Philadelphia Orchestra in 1929. This transfer preserves the movement’s first 78-rpm side.

sections.label: Intro · Muted strings find E major
sections.mNote: Slow chords connect C minor with the new key

sections.label: A · Flute and clarinet over piano
sections.mNote: The long melody unfolds above circling arpeggios

sections.label: B · The opening song continues
sections.mNote: Piano and orchestra share the E major melody

cues.title: Four bars between two keys
cues.text: Muted strings begin in C minor, the key of the first movement. Their slow chords move by semitones towards E major; clarinets, bassoons and horns join them. The piano waits until the new key is ready.
cues.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, p. 48: four-bar introduction, muted strings, wind entries and piano entrance in E major. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP528309-PMLP01953-Rachmaninoff_-_Piano_Concerto_No._2_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute, then clarinet
cues.text: The piano’s arpeggios circle quietly beneath a wind melody. A flute begins the phrase; a clarinet continues it, marked dolce e sempre espressivo — sweetly, always expressive. Rachmaninoff gives the soloist the moving notes and the wind players time to breathe.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 48–49, rehearsal 17: piano arpeggios, solo flute and clarinet continuation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first take survives
cues.text: At the Academy of Music in Philadelphia on 10 April 1929, Rachmaninoff and Stokowski record two takes of this Adagio opening. The first becomes the master; the second is destroyed. The issued side carries the music on HMV D.B. 1334.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor matrix CVE-48966: date, venue, take 1 master, take 2 destroyed and DB-1334 issue. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800022752

cues.title: A charity concert in Moscow
cues.text: On 15 December 1900 Rachmaninoff plays this Adagio and the finale in Moscow, with Alexander Siloti conducting. The concert raises money for prisoners through the Ladies’ Charity Prison Committee. The first movement is still unfinished.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note documents the date, performers, charity and order of the concerto’s completion. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
